notes.text: Sydney sees a total solar eclipse; the next one visible there is on 3 June 2858, eight hundred and thirty years later.
Between 10,000 and 15,000 time capsules are buried worldwide - objects people made specifically to be opened by the centuries this story is about.

centuryFacts.text: 235 solar eclipses: 79 partial, 87 annular, 65 total, 4 hybrid. The longest totality of the century lasts 7 m 29 s, on 16 July 2186.

248 solar eclipses: 92 partial, 86 annular, 67 total, 3 hybrid. The longest totality is 7 m 22 s, on 27 July 2204 - and 2204 has two of the century's extremes in one year, a 10 m 38 s annular in February and that total in July.
225 solar eclipses: 83 partial, 72 annular, 64 total, 6 hybrid. The longest totality is 7 m 12 s, on 25 June 2522.

projected.text: The world is as it was in 2026, continuing: warmer, more crowded, more connected. The numbers come from the UN and the climate reports, and they stop being numbers at 2100.
The sea is higher than it was. Cities near the coast have moved back or built up. Nothing in the record says what the people here call themselves now.
The ruins of the twentieth century are still being dug up. The languages spoken are not the ones written on those ruins.
The old cities are mounds. Their names are known to scholars, not to the people living on them.
The twentieth century is as distant as Sumer is to us. What survives of it is stone, plastic and a few written languages nobody speaks.

authored.text: The annular eclipse crosses the ocean and misses India entirely, but every phone in the old city shows the same live picture, and a crowd gathers anyway. That is the year it becomes ordinary to know exactly when the sky will do something - not as prophecy, as a calendar. The priests at the temple do not argue with it. They have been keeping their own calendar longer than anyone can remember, and it has never once been wrong about the moon.

authored.text: The total eclipse of 2 August 2027 is the longest over land this century. A schoolteacher from Hyderabad saves for two years to stand under it, in Egypt, and afterwards cannot describe it without becoming annoying. She brings back a photograph, a stone, and a notebook full of times. The notebook is the thing that survives - three hundred years later it is still the oldest object in the room.

authored.text: 1999 AN10 passes at 388,960 km - close enough to be news, far enough to be nothing. Somebody builds an app that tells you, hour by hour, how far away it is. It becomes the most-downloaded thing in the city for eleven days, and then nobody opens it again. This is how ordinary a computable future feels: you check it, you shrug, you put it down.

authored.text: The big one of the decade: Apophis comes closer than the television satellites. On rooftops across the Deccan people wait, and at the appointed minute it slides across the sky - bright, unhurried, exactly where the tables said. A man who sells bangles says his grandfather was told, by a book, that the end would come from the sky in his lifetime. It did not. This is better: a stone, on time, doing nothing. He goes back to selling bangles.

authored.text: The largest total lunar eclipse of the century. The Moon goes the colour of a lamp seen through a sari, and stays that way long enough for people to stop being impressed and start talking about other things - which is, in the end, what makes an evening remembered. A boy asks why it is red. His uncle says dust. His grandmother says something else. Both are given, and the boy keeps both.

authored.text: The stage of the rocket that took men to the Moon in 1969 is back in Earth's orbit, drifting home after six decades around the Sun. Somebody points a telescope at it and shows a class of children a cylinder of American paint turning over in the dark. The children are not moved - it is a thing, not a monument - but their teacher writes in the log: 'first object of the old century to return'. She is wrong; it will be the first of many. She is right that it is worth logging.

authored.text: An annular eclipse crosses the peninsula in the morning, and for six minutes the sun is a ring that everyone photographs badly. Schools close, not from fear but because nobody wants to teach through it. Two boys burn a pinhole in a bus ticket and the whole street learns in an hour what an eye should never look at directly. The ticket goes into a drawer. It will outlast the street.

authored.chapter: The book that was dug up
authored.text: A date from an old book: the palm leaves are supposed to come out of their pit here, and the man who was supposed to come does not. The pit is in a courtyard behind the matham. A hundred people come anyway, and what they get is a village festival and a long argument between two families about whose courtyard it actually is. The leaves stay where they are. The argument is written down by somebody's cousin, and that writing outlives the festival.

authored.chapter: The war that did not come
authored.text: The month a war was foretold, a hundred years of prediction meeting one ordinary Tuesday. No war. In a bookshop in the old quarter the proprietor moves the book from the front shelf to a lower one, as his father did in 2011, and as the man before him did in 2024. In the margin he writes the date of the next prediction, and under it, in smaller letters: 'this is how it stays alive'.

authored.chapter: The day every country did not surrender
authored.text: Today, some said, the world's nations would lay down their sovereignty to a king. Instead a district court sits late, a boundary dispute between two villages is settled in favour of the smaller one, and the losing side files an appeal. Nine hundred people are affected. It is not a kingdom. It is administration, which is slower and less photogenic and, on the whole, harder to get wrong.

authored.text: Halley's Comet, back after seventy-five years. Telescopes on the school roof, a queue down the stairs, a great deal of noise, and somebody's grandmother in a plastic chair at the back saying she saw it in 1986 and it was better then. She is almost certainly wrong, and everybody lets her have it. Nobody in that queue will see it again. A few of them understand that at the time, and are quiet for a minute, and then are not.

authored.text: The tables of population and sea level end in 2100, and after that the archives hold no totals worth the name. People keep counting - births, deaths, sacks of grain - but the counts no longer add up to a story anyone can check. A student finds a chart of the 2090s and cannot tell whether the line goes up or down at the edge. She writes in the margin: 'beyond here, believe nobody, including me.'

authored.text: The longest totality of the century, seven minutes and twenty-nine seconds. Nobody in the city has ever seen anything like it and nobody ever will. What gets written down, though, is not the eclipse. It is that the tables were right - again, after a hundred and sixty years, through whatever happened in between, kept in some form by somebody. The arithmetic is what survives a civilisation. The rest is argument, and the argument is what people enjoy.

authored.text: A total eclipse of seven minutes and twelve seconds. People come from three weeks' travel away. The city they arrive in is a mound with a well in it recently re-dug, a wall of reused railway sleepers, and a name that survives only in a copied list. The visitors are not disappointed. They came for the sky, which is the only thing that has never once lied to them about where it will be.

authored.text: A city on the far side of the world finally gets its second total eclipse, eight and a half centuries after the first. The records of the 2028 one have been copied so many times that the copies disagree about the crowd, the weather and the year, but not about the date or the time. That is the pattern of everything this story has been about: the sky keeps its appointments and people keep arguing about what it meant.

authored.text: Halley returns, as it has every seventy-five years since before there were cities here. Nobody living has seen it. Somewhere in the chain of copying there is a line - the date and the hour - that came from a notebook of times kept by a schoolteacher who travelled to Egypt in 2027. The note is gone. The numbers are not. Of everything this millennium made, the arithmetic is what survived.

authored.text: The summit of the Charminar is a stone platform with a view and a name that half the people using it cannot spell. The astronomers of this year have eclipse tables as good as ours, and can name the day the sun went out over the Deccan in 2035 - to the minute, with the weather unknown. Of the people who stood in it, they know only that there were many, that somebody brought a bus ticket with a pinhole in it, and that this, somehow, survived. It is in a case. The card says what it is. The card is wrong about two things and right about one, which is better than most of what we will leave.
